bibliographic.authors: Kai-Jen Chuang, Lian-Yu Lin, Kin-Fai Ho, Chien-Tien Su
bibliographic.title: Traffic-related PM2.5 exposure and its cardiovascular effects among healthy commuters in Taipei, Taiwan
bibliographic.volumeIssuePages: Volume 7, article 100084 (5 pages). Received 20 April 2020; revised 1 July 2020; accepted 4 July 2020; available online 5 July 2020
bibliographic.funding: Grant MOST 106-EPA-F-014-001- from the Ministry of Science and Technology of Taiwan; funders had no role in design, analysis or publication. Authors declare no competing interests.

studyDesign: Panel study in Taipei, Taiwan, 1 Feb 2017 to 31 Dec 2019, 0900-1000 h. 120 healthy never-smoking adults aged 20-30 (mean 24.8; BMI 22.7), recruited by oral invitation from earlier panels, classified by their own commuting style into six modes (electric subway; gasoline bus, car, scooter; walking; walking with 3M 8812 respirator). 720 1-h measurements of personal PM2.5 (Grimm DUST-check 1.108), noise (B&K 4443), temperature, humidity, plus SBP, DBP, HR every 15 min (DynaPulse 5000A, 1-h mean) and post-measurement urinary 8-OHdG. Table 1 lists 20 participants per mode; the paper does not reconcile this with 'six measurements per participant in six modes'. Mixed-effects models (nlme), PM2.5 1-h mean as predictor, adjusted for age, sex, BMI, order, temperature, humidity, noise (and mode in Model 1); effects as percent change per IQR of PM2.5. Only PM2.5 mass measured; no CO, VOCs, NO2, ozone, particle number or exertion. Route, distance, vehicle type and traffic not described.

findings.claim: The study enrolled 120 healthy, never-smoking young adults in Taipei and took 720 one-hour measurements.
findings.value: n=120; mean age 24.8 y (SD 0.1 as printed), range 20-30; BMI 22.7 kg/m2 (SD 0.9); 59 men and 61 women by Table 1; 720 1-h measurements; 1 Feb 2017 to 31 Dec 2019; 0900-1000 h
findings.quote: We recruited 120 healthy commuters ... Each participant conducted six 1-h measurements, resulting in a total of 720 1-h measurements from February 1, 2017 to December 31, 2019.
findings.caveats: Table 1 lists exactly 20 participants per mode and the mode groups differ in sex ratio and mean age (car 27.9 y, 13 men), which suggests different people in different modes, yet Methods/abstract say six measurements in six modes. The paper does not reconcile this. Healthy young adults only; recruited by oral invitation from earlier panels.
findings.useOnSite: The study followed 120 healthy young adults in Taipei, with 720 one-hour measurements made between 9 and 10 am over 2017-2019.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers match. Added sex count (10+8+13+10+10+8 = 59 men) and BMI SD. Design ambiguity retained: it is unclear whether each person did one mode x 6 repeats or all six modes once.

findings.claim: Riders of gasoline scooters had the highest mean personal PM2.5 of the six modes.
findings.quote: Table 1, PM2.5: Scooter (Sc) 53.6 ± 26.1; IQR 41.7; Range 22.8-92.3
findings.significance: ANOVA p=0.04 (printed on the IQR row of the PM2.5 block). Scheffe pairs listed: Sc/S; Sc/C; W/S; W/C; WM/S; WM/C. Scooter vs bus, vs walking and vs masked walking are NOT listed as significant.
findings.caveats: Measures the rider, not a pedestrian. Scooter is gasoline-powered (Methods and abstract). Total PM2.5 mass only. Highest mean, but not shown to differ significantly from walking or bus.
findings.useOnSite: Gasoline-scooter riders in Taipei had a mean personal PM2.5 of 53.6 µg/m³ over a morning commute hour, the highest mean of six modes (significantly higher than subway and car; not significantly different from walking or bus).
findings.checkerNote: Number is right. Site wording tightened: the paper does not show scooter riders significantly higher than walkers or bus users.

findings.claim: Pedestrians walking without a mask had a mean personal PM2.5 well above subway and car commuters.
findings.quote: Table 1, PM2.5: Walking (W) 42.7 ± 22.6; IQR 24.4; Range 19.2-78.2
findings.significance: Scheffe: W/S and W/C significant; W vs bus not listed. Text (p.2) says 2.0-fold the subway mean.
findings.caveats: Rank: scooter 53.6 > walking with facemask 43.1 > walking 42.7 > bus 34.7 > car 26.2 > subway 21.7, so unmasked walking is second-highest only among modes without a mask. The p.3 Discussion says walkers exceeded 'subway, bus and car', but the Scheffe list has no W/B pair. Route not described; mean of a 1-h walk, not a crosswalk measurement. Nothing links walkers' PM2.5 to scooters.
findings.useOnSite: Pedestrians walking in Taipei morning traffic had a mean personal PM2.5 of 42.7 µg/m³, about twice the subway commuters' level.
findings.checkerNote: Reader's 'second-highest' ranking was ambiguous (masked walkers, 43.1, are nominally higher); clarified. Walking-vs-bus not significant per Table 1.

findings.claim: Subway commuters (electric rail) had the lowest personal PM2.5.
findings.quote: Table 1 PM2.5, Subway (S): 21.7 ± 5.8; IQR 14.7; Range 8.6-32.5
findings.caveats: Electric subway, not an electric scooter. The authors cite their own earlier study (Liu et al. 2015) which found the highest PM2.5 in the subway, so the ranking is not universal.
findings.useOnSite: Commuters on the electric subway had the lowest PM2.5 of the six modes, at 21.7 µg/m³.
findings.checkerNote: Checked against the PDF table image. Removed stray key 'useOnse'.

findings.claim: Bus and car occupants had intermediate PM2.5 levels.
findings.significance: Car significantly lower than scooter and walking (Sc/C, W/C).
findings.caveats: Authors attribute low in-car levels to ventilation, filtration and air conditioning (p.4); not tested here. The bus is labelled gasoline-powered in Methods.
findings.useOnSite: People inside cars (26.2) and buses (34.7) had lower mean personal PM2.5 than those on scooters or on foot.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers match Table 1.

findings.claim: PM2.5 around walkers wearing a respirator was no lower than around walkers without one because the monitor was outside the mask.
findings.quote: we could only measure PM2.5 exposure levels around participants but not PM2.5 exposure levels in the facemasks
findings.significance: WM/S and WM/C significant vs subway and car.
findings.caveats: Not a measure of inhaled dose; the inhaled concentration for mask wearers is unmeasured. Authors say the 3M 8812 'theoretically' filters at least 95% of PM2.5.
findings.useOnSite: The facemask result cannot be read as exposure inside the mask, since the monitor sat outside it.
findings.checkerNote: Correct. Quote is on p.4.

findings.claim: Scooter and walking mean PM2.5 were 2.5-fold and 2.0-fold the subway mean.
findings.quote: The levels of PM2.5 in the scooter mode and the walking mode were 2.5-fold and 2.0-fold higher than those in the subway mode
findings.significance: No test reported for the ratios.
findings.caveats: Ratios of group means: 53.6/21.7 = 2.47, 42.7/21.7 = 1.97 (checker arithmetic). Note the authors use 'fold higher' inconsistently within the same paragraph (see mode-health-levels).
findings.useOnSite: Scooter riders' mean PM2.5 was about 2.5 times, and pedestrians' about 2 times, that of subway commuters.
findings.checkerNote: Value and page confirmed; caveat on the paper's inconsistent 'fold higher' usage added.

findings.claim: Unadjusted mean BP, HR and 8-OHdG during the hour were higher in scooter and walking modes than in subway mode.
findings.significance: ANOVA p=0.04 (SBP), 0.04 (DBP), 0.05 (HR), 0.01 (8-OHdG). Scheffe: SBP Sc/S, Sc/C, Sc/WM, W/S, W/WM; DBP Sc/S, W/S; HR Sc/S only (walking vs subway HR not significant); 8-OHdG Sc/S, Sc/C, Sc/WM, W/S, W/C, W/WM.
findings.caveats: Between-mode raw means, unadjusted, confounded by exertion, noise and person. Text (p.2): scooter SBP/DBP/8-OHdG '27%, 35% and 5.1-fold higher', walking '17%, 21% and 3.8-fold higher' than subway. Table ratios: SBP 143/113=1.27, DBP 97/72=1.35, 8-OHdG 3.7/0.6=6.2; walking 132/113=1.17, 87/72=1.21, 2.9/0.6=4.8. So the 8-OHdG figures are 'excess over subway' (6.2-1 and 4.8-1, allowing rounding), not ratios, whereas the PM2.5 '2.5-fold' is a ratio. Mean scooter SBP of 143 mmHg in healthy young adults is notably high and presumably reflects the commute situation; the paper does not discuss it. HR unit printed as 'beats/hour' in text and table (evidently per minute).
findings.useOnSite: Unadjusted averages during the commute hour were higher among scooter riders and walkers than subway commuters, but these differences also reflect exertion, noise and who chooses each mode.
findings.checkerNote: Reader flagged the 8-OHdG text/table mismatch as an error; it is better explained as a 'fold higher' = ratio minus 1 convention. Scheffe pairs per endpoint added; walking vs subway HR not significant.

findings.claim: In scooter mode, one IQR higher PM2.5 was associated with significantly higher SBP, HR and 8-OHdG, but not DBP.
findings.significance: * printed on SBP, HR, 8-OHdG; the note does not define the asterisk; CIs for those three exclude zero.
findings.caveats: IQR is the scooter mode's own (41.7), not per 10 µg/m3. Percent change is relative to M, 'the mean of each cardiovascular endpoint' (not stated whether overall or mode-specific mean); no absolute mmHg or bpm. Random-effects structure not stated. SBP lower CI limit 0.9 is marginal. Exposure and outcome measured in the same hour. Riders of gasoline scooters, healthy young adults.
findings.useOnSite: Among scooter riders, a rise in PM2.5 of 41.7 µg/m³ (one IQR) was associated with 7.9% higher systolic BP, 6.4% higher heart rate and 8.9% higher urinary 8-OHdG, in the same hour.
findings.checkerNote: Matches the PDF table image.

findings.claim: In walking mode, one IQR higher PM2.5 was associated with significantly higher SBP, HR and 8-OHdG; DBP shows a negative association whose CI excludes zero but is not asterisked.
findings.locator: Table 2, Model 6 (read from the PDF page image; the text layer drops minus signs)
findings.significance: Asterisks on SBP, HR, 8-OHdG. The DBP CI (-5.2, -1.6) excludes zero, in the negative direction; the paper does not discuss it.
findings.caveats: The reader's note that the DBP minus sign was missing is wrong: the printed value is -3.4. The point estimate lies inside the CI. The HR (3.4; 0.1, 3.5) and 8-OHdG (8.1; 0.7, 8.8) intervals are strongly asymmetric around the estimate, which is unusual for a symmetric CI and may be a typographical error; treat their precision cautiously. Walking route and the source of walkers' PM2.5 are not described.
findings.useOnSite: Among pedestrians, a rise of 24.4 µg/m³ PM2.5 (one IQR) was associated with 6.5% higher systolic BP and 8.1% higher urinary 8-OHdG in the same hour; the HR and 8-OHdG intervals as printed look irregular.
findings.checkerNote: DBP is -3.4 (-5.2, -1.6), not 3.4 with a missing minus. Authors' text does not say DBP was non-significant; it is simply unstarred and undiscussed. Asymmetric HR and 8-OHdG CIs kept as flagged.

findings.claim: In the electric subway, no significant association of PM2.5 with SBP, DBP, HR or 8-OHdG.
findings.caveats: Narrow exposure range (8.6-32.5) and a smaller IQR limit power; a null is not proof of no effect. Subway is electric rail, not an electric scooter.
findings.useOnSite: Where PM2.5 stayed low and in a narrow range (subway), no association with BP, heart rate or 8-OHdG was found.
findings.checkerNote: Matches.

findings.claim: In car mode, no significant association with BP or HR; a small significant 8-OHdG association.
findings.caveats: Text (p.4) says 'a mild increase (2.3%) in urinary 8-OHdG in the car mode and walking mode wearing a facemask'; Table 2 gives 1.8% for car and 2.3% for facemask walking. Internal inconsistency in the paper. Cars were gasoline-powered, often air-conditioned.
findings.useOnSite: Car occupants showed little BP or heart-rate association; only a small 8-OHdG association.
findings.checkerNote: Matches table; text/table discrepancy confirmed.

findings.claim: In bus mode, PM2.5 was associated with higher SBP and 8-OHdG; HR and DBP point estimates were negative.
findings.significance: SBP and 8-OHdG asterisked. HR CI (-3.3, -1.3) excludes zero (a decrease) but is unstarred and undiscussed.
findings.caveats: The bus HR interval is internally consistent (estimate inside CI), so 'probable misprint' is not established; the paper simply does not comment. Buses are labelled gasoline-powered in Methods; the Introduction discusses diesel buses only from other studies.
findings.useOnSite: Bus riders showed an association with systolic BP (+4.6% per IQR of 22.6 µg/m3) and 8-OHdG (+3.1%).
findings.checkerNote: Removed the 'misprint' assumption for bus HR; flagged as an unstarred, undiscussed negative association.

findings.claim: For walkers wearing a respirator, no significant PM2.5 association with BP or HR, but a small 8-OHdG association.
findings.quote: Model 7: Subjects in walking mode wearing a facemask 2.3(-4.8, 9.4) -2.9 (-14.4, 8.6) -6.8(-17.9, 4.3) 2.3*(0.2, 4.4)
findings.caveats: Exposure was measured outside the mask, so this does not show what the mask wearer inhaled. Authors note mask discomfort could raise BP and HR. This is a mask result, not about electric vehicles.
findings.useOnSite: Among walkers wearing a respirator, associations with BP and heart rate were not significant; 8-OHdG was (+2.3%).
findings.checkerNote: Chain link changed from '7-electric' to 'context': a facemask is not a tailpipe-removal measure. Numbers confirmed.

findings.claim: With all 720 measurements pooled across modes (Model 1, adjusted also for mode), only 8-OHdG was significantly associated with PM2.5.
findings.significance: 8-OHdG CI excludes zero; SBP, DBP, HR include zero.
findings.caveats: The paper does not say which IQR the pooled model uses. The abstract does not report this null for BP and HR in all subjects. Text (p.3) also says 'The commuting mode was significantly associated with PM2.5 in Model 1' without further detail.
findings.useOnSite: Across all commute modes pooled, PM2.5 was associated with higher 8-OHdG (4.7% per IQR) but not significantly with BP or heart rate.
findings.checkerNote: Matches.

findings.claim: No DBP association was starred as significant in any mode; two unstarred estimates (walking DBP, bus HR) have CIs excluding zero in the negative direction.
findings.quote: Table 2 DBP column, Models 1-7
findings.significance: No DBP asterisks. Walking DBP CI (-5.2, -1.6) excludes zero but the estimate is negative (lower DBP with higher PM2.5).
findings.caveats: Reader's statement that all DBP CIs include zero is wrong for walking. Negative estimates are not discussed by the authors, and none of the many estimates is corrected for multiplicity.
findings.useOnSite: No significant increase in diastolic BP with PM2.5 was found in any mode.
findings.checkerNote: Reader said all DBP CIs include zero or are misprinted; walking DBP CI excludes zero on the negative side. Reworded to 'no significant increase'.

findings.claim: Noise was highest on scooters and was measured and adjusted for.
findings.quote: Table 1 Noise, dBA: Scooter 89.3 ± 12.6; Text: 'The mean noise levels remained under 90 dBA in all commuting modes.'
findings.caveats: Noise is adjusted in all models, but scooter noise and PM2.5 are both highest in the same mode. Walking maximum (111.5 dBA) exceeds the scooter maximum (110.8). Reader omitted the masked-walking row.
findings.useOnSite: The study measured noise and adjusted for it, but noise was highest on scooters (mean 89.3 dBA).
findings.checkerNote: Added masked-walking noise row, walking maximum, and the text's 'under 90 dBA' statement (page 2).

findings.claim: Models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, order of measurement, temperature, humidity and noise (plus mode in Model 1).
findings.quote: All models (Model 1 to 7) were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), order of the measurement, 1-h temperature, 1-h humidity and 1-h noise level.
findings.caveats: Physical exertion, CO, NO2, VOCs and ozone were not measured or controlled (p.4). ETS and time-activity were recorded by questionnaire (p.2) but not listed as covariates. The effect formula is printed as [β × IQR × M] × 100% with M the endpoint mean (the multiplication by M is probably a typo for division).
findings.useOnSite: The analysis adjusted for noise and weather but not for physical exertion or other pollutants.
findings.checkerNote: Matches. Printed formula quirk added.

findings.claim: The paper does not measure tailpipe emissions or attribute PM2.5 to scooter exhaust; it names scooters/motorcycles in its abstract recommendation and in citing other studies.
findings.quote: We encourage commuters to commute using public rapid transit systems instead of riding scooters/motorcycles during rush hours.
findings.locator: Abstract (the Section 5 wording ends 'instead of riding scooters/motorcycles.')
findings.caveats: 'Traffic-related PM2.5' is total PM2.5 mass; no apportionment, speciation, benzene, CO or hydrocarbons. The Discussion cites Li et al. 2017 on motorcyclists.
findings.useOnSite: The paper measures total PM2.5 only and does not identify scooter exhaust as the source of walkers' PM2.5.
findings.checkerNote: The 'during rush hours' phrase is from the abstract; the Section 5 sentence omits it.

findings.claim: Authors explain lower PM2.5 in subway and car by ventilation and in-vehicle filtration.
findings.quote: These findings suggest that the ventilation status of the vehicle is an important factor for TRAP exposure. The in-vehicle filtration system can reduce the penetration of outdoor air pollutants
findings.caveats: Not tested in this study; the same paragraph cites an earlier study by the authors that found the highest PM2.5 in the subway.
findings.useOnSite: The authors attribute low car levels to filtration and ventilation.
findings.checkerNote: Matches.

findings.claim: Authors propose a mechanism from cited literature.
findings.quote: may involve the passage of inhaled particles into the lungs and blood circulation, inducing pulmonary inflammation and oxidative stress, activating pulmonary neural reflexes, and initiating autonomic function imbalance (Brook et al., 2010)
findings.caveats: Not tested here; the authors state the clinical meaning of short-term fluctuations is unknown.
findings.useOnSite: The authors cite an American Heart Association statement for the mechanism.
findings.checkerNote: Matches.

findings.claim: Authors conclude scooter riders and pedestrians were at increased cardiovascular risk and recommend rapid transit over scooters/motorcycles.
findings.quote: Such findings suggest that scooter riders and pedestrians were at increased risks for cardiovascular effects from high-level PM2.5 exposure compared with subway passengers, car drivers and pedestrians with facemasks.
findings.caveats: Risk inferred from short-term marker changes; no clinical outcomes. No electric scooter studied. The sentence follows the authors' citations of mask and filtration studies.
findings.useOnSite: The authors recommend public rapid transit, not electric scooters.
findings.checkerNote: Matches.

findings.claim: Health measures were taken in the same hour as exposure; no lag or persistence was assessed.
findings.value: BP/HR every 15 min during the 1-h commute; urine collected after each measurement
findings.quote: We recorded each participant's SBP, DBP and HR every 15 min during all 1-h measurements ... After each measurement, we collected a 10-mL urine sample
findings.caveats: The delay before urine collection and any follow-up are not stated.
findings.useOnSite: The associations are for the same hour as the commute; the paper does not show how long effects last.
findings.checkerNote: Matches.

findings.claim: The study commute is a fixed 1-h window 0900-1000, not a measured trip length.
findings.quote: during 1-h morning commutes (0900-1000 h)
findings.caveats: Introduction (p.1) says Taiwan daily commute is 50 min, citing Dalia Research (2016); the reference list entry for that source is titled about LGBT identification in Europe, so the citation appears wrong and should not be relied on.
findings.useOnSite: Exposure was measured over one morning hour.
findings.checkerNote: Added reference-list anomaly.

findings.claim: 8-OHdG is described as a stable oxidative-stress marker associated with cardiovascular risk.
findings.quote: Urinary 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) has been reported to be a stable marker of oxidative stress and be associated with increases in cardiovascular risk
findings.caveats: No creatinine adjustment is mentioned.
findings.useOnSite: 8-OHdG is a marker of oxidative stress; the study shows association, not disease.
findings.checkerNote: Matches.

findings.claim: The sample excludes children, older people and people with disease; authors caution against extrapolation.
findings.quote: the participants are healthy, young commuters. Therefore, our findings may not be completely extrapolated to other locations with different commuters' characteristics, environmental, and meteorological conditions.
findings.caveats: No children, strollers, older adults or roadside workers studied.
findings.useOnSite: The study is in healthy young adults; it did not test children or older people.
findings.checkerNote: Matches.

findings.claim: A cited Taipei study (Li et al. 2017) reported far higher PM2.5 inhaled by motorcyclists than walkers.
findings.quote: motorcycling: 3340.8 μg/m3; bicycling: 1090.2 μg/m3; walking: 133.4 μg/m3
findings.caveats: Cited, not this study's data; described as based on spatial interpolation of EPA station data and 'pollutant doses' with 'short-duration peaks'. The units look like a dose, not a concentration.
findings.useOnSite: Do not use without checking Li et al. 2017 directly.
findings.checkerNote: Matches the text as cited; keep out of site copy.

findings.claim: Several pairwise PM2.5 differences that the site might assume are not listed as significant.
findings.value: Scheffe list for PM2.5: Sc/S; Sc/C; W/S; W/C; WM/S; WM/C only
findings.quote: Table 1 Scheffe's test, PM2.5 row: Sc/S; Sc/C; W/S; W/C; WM/S; WM/C
findings.significance: Scooter vs walking, scooter vs bus, walking vs bus: not listed as significant.
findings.caveats: Means differ (53.6 vs 42.7 vs 34.7) but the paper does not show these differences are statistically distinguishable.
findings.useOnSite: Say scooter and walking were both higher than subway and car, rather than that scooter riders were higher than pedestrians.
findings.checkerNote: Reader noted this partly; made explicit.

findings.claim: Walkers with a respirator had similar PM2.5 outside the mask but lower mean SBP and 8-OHdG than unmasked walkers.
findings.value: SBP 116 ± 9.7 vs 132 ± 11.9 mmHg; 8-OHdG 1.4 ± 0.7 vs 2.9 ± 1.3 ng/ml; PM2.5 outside 43.1 vs 42.7
findings.quote: participants wearing a facemask in walking mode had relatively lower SBP responses and urinary 8-OHdG levels than the participants without a facemask in walking mode (ANOVA, p-value < 0.05)
findings.significance: Scheffe: SBP W/WM; 8-OHdG W/WM; HR and DBP not different.
findings.caveats: Unadjusted between-group means, probably different people; mask effects on inhaled dose were not measured.
findings.useOnSite: Not a site claim about electric vehicles; at most a note that the authors found lower raw SBP and 8-OHdG with a mask.
findings.checkerNote: Missed by reader; relevant to interpreting the mask results.

findings.claim: Two unstarred estimates have CIs entirely below zero.
findings.significance: CI excludes zero in the negative direction; no asterisk; not discussed.
findings.caveats: Shows irregular reporting in Table 2 and that not every association points in the harmful direction.
findings.useOnSite: Do not quote these as effects; mention only if discussing data quality.
findings.checkerNote: Reader missed that walking DBP is negative.

limitations: Authors: 'The major limitation of our panel study was the biological explanation of the short-term effects of PM2.5 on cardiovascular endpoints.' (p.4)
Authors: 'whether short-term and small fluctuations of cardiovascular endpoints are associated with higher risks of cardiovascular diseases clinically remains unknown.' (p.4)
Authors: 'The physical activities were completely different among commuters of different commuting modes, resulting in confounding effects.' (p.4)
Authors: mask discomfort 'might indirectly result in increased BP and HR and subsequently confound the observed associations.' (p.4)
Authors: personal data on 'nitrogen dioxide, volatile organic compounds, and ozone' were unavailable; these 'might bias our study results toward the null.' (p.4)
Authors: only healthy young commuters in subtropical Taipei; findings 'may not be completely extrapolated to other locations'. (p.4)
Authors: PM2.5 could be measured only around, not inside, the facemask. (p.4)
Checker: participants' modes were their own commuting style (self-selection); not randomised.
Checker: design unclear (Table 1 shows 20 per mode with differing age and sex mix, Methods say six modes per person); random-effects structure not stated.

Checker: effect sizes are per mode-specific IQR (14.7 to 41.7 µg/m3), not comparable between modes; no per-10 µg/m3 estimate; no absolute mmHg or bpm; M (endpoint mean) not specified as overall or per-mode.
Checker: no multiplicity correction stated; 28 estimates in Table 2, several significant at CI edges; some unstarred CIs exclude zero.
Checker: total PM2.5 only, low-cost optical monitor, calibration not described; no speciation, CO, benzene, VOC or particle number; no source apportionment.
Checker: exposure and outcomes measured in the same hour; no lag, persistence or reversibility assessed.
Checker: Table 2 has asymmetric CIs (walking HR, walking 8-OHdG) and text/table discrepancies (car 8-OHdG 2.3% vs 1.8%).
Checker: Supplementary data (Appendix A) are referenced but not in the supplied PDF and were not read.
complications: Scooters in this paper are gasoline-powered and the participants are riders, not pedestrians beside scooters; there is no tailpipe measurement, no electric-scooter comparison, and no attribution of walkers' PM2.5 to scooters.

The only cleaner alternative studied is the electrically powered subway (and mostly air-conditioned cars); electric scooters were not studied, so the paper cannot support 'switch to electric scooters' directly. The authors recommend public rapid transit.

Physical exertion was not measured or adjusted for; walking and scooter modes differ in exertion, noise and posture, and the authors say this confounds BP and HR comparisons. Mean scooter SBP was 143 mmHg.
Noise was highest on scooters (89.3 dBA mean) and is adjusted for, but noise and PM2.5 co-vary across modes.
Pooled analysis (Model 1) found no significant PM2.5 association with SBP, DBP or HR, only with 8-OHdG.
No DBP association is starred; walking DBP is -3.4% (-5.2, -1.6) and bus HR -2.3% (-3.3, -1.3), unstarred and undiscussed negative estimates.
Scooter, walking and bus PM2.5 are not shown to differ significantly from each other (Scheffe list); only vs subway and car.
Facemask and subway modes show no BP/HR association, but exposure ranges are narrow and facemask exposure was measured outside the mask.
Table 1 shows 20 participants per mode, in tension with the Methods statement that each person did all six modes (720 measurements).

Table 1 age SDs (0.1-0.2 y) are implausible for a range of 20-30 y and inconsistent with the car group's mean age of 27.9 y alongside ANOVA p=0.72; BMI SDs also very small; HR unit is printed 'beats/hour'.
Text 'fold higher' is used as a ratio for PM2.5 (2.5-fold) but as ratio minus 1 for 8-OHdG (5.1-fold vs a table ratio of 6.2).
Table 2 has irregular intervals (walking HR 3.4 with CI 0.1-3.5; walking 8-OHdG 8.1 with CI 0.7-8.8) and car 8-OHdG is 1.8% in the table but 2.3% in text.
The study hour (0900-1000) is called 'rush hour' by the authors, but no traffic counts are given; the Taiwan commute-time citation (Dalia Research 2016) is listed with an unrelated title.
Walkers' 42.7 µg/m3 is a 1-h mean over an unspecified route; it does not describe a red-light crosswalk, idling or queues of scooters, none of which were measured.
The authors' earlier study (Liu 2015) found the highest PM2.5 in the subway, so the mode ranking is context-dependent.
correctionsToAbstractLevelNotes: The abstract gives percent changes without the increment; the full text shows they are per IQR of each mode's own PM2.5 (scooter 41.7, walking 24.4 µg/m3), not per 10 µg/m3 and not comparable across modes.
The abstract highlights walking and scooter results; the full text shows the pooled all-mode model (Model 1) was significant for 8-OHdG only.

The abstract says no significance for subway; the text adds that car mode had no SBP/DBP/HR association and bus mode had SBP and 8-OHdG significant; car, bus and facemask modes showed small 8-OHdG associations (1.8%, 3.1%, 2.3%).
The abstract's facemask statement (no significant association with BP and HR) holds, but 8-OHdG was significant (+2.3%).
Table 2 walking DBP is -3.4% (-5.2, -1.6), a negative estimate; walking HR and 8-OHdG intervals are asymmetric.
The abstract gives only scooter and subway PM2.5; walking is 42.7 ± 22.6 µg/m3 (19.2-78.2).
The abstract does not give Table 1 group means for BP, HR, 8-OHdG, noise, or state that exertion and other pollutants were uncontrolled.
The abstract says each participant had six repeated measurements in six modes; Table 1 shows 20 people per mode.
'Scooter' means gasoline scooter riders; no source apportionment exists.
answersToQuestions: 1. Design: 120 healthy never-smoking adults aged 20-30 (mean 24.8, SD 0.1 as printed; BMI 22.7 ± 0.9), 59 men and 61 women, recruited by the PI's oral invitation from previous panels in Taipei. 'Participants were classified with different commuting modes according to their own commuting style' (self-selected, not randomised). Six modes: electric subway, gasoline bus, gasoline car, gasoline scooter, walking, walking with a 3M 8812 respirator. 'Each participant conducted six 1-h measurements' (720 total), 0900-1000 h, 1 Feb 2017 to 31 Dec 2019; Table 1 shows 20 people per mode, unreconciled. Route, distance, vehicle type and traffic not described. Instruments: Grimm DUST-check 1.108 (PM2.5, temperature, humidity), B&K 4443 noise dosimeter, DynaPulse 5000A (SBP, DBP, HR every 15 min, four readings averaged), 10-mL urine after each measurement for 8-OHdG by commercial kit.

2. Personal PM2.5 (Table 1, p.3, mean ± SD; range): subway 21.7 ± 5.8 (8.6-32.5); car 26.2 ± 12.5 (1.8-56.2); bus 34.7 ± 15.1 (2.2-61.9); walking 42.7 ± 22.6 (19.2-78.2); walking with respirator 43.1 ± 20.7 (18.7-81.4, outside the mask); scooter 53.6 ± 26.1 (22.8-92.3). IQRs 14.7, 16.1, 22.6, 24.4, 25.8, 41.7. ANOVA p=0.04. Scheffe significant pairs: Sc/S, Sc/C, W/S, W/C, WM/S, WM/C; scooter vs walking and vs bus, and walking vs bus, not listed. Walking is a 1-h mean on an unspecified route.

3. Effects (Table 2, p.3), percent change per IQR of 1-h PM2.5, as in the chart-ready Table B. Scooter (IQR 41.7): SBP 7.9 (0.9, 14.9), DBP 0.6 (-11.9, 13.1), HR 6.4 (2.6, 10.2), 8-OHdG 8.9 (2.6, 15.2). Walking (IQR 24.4): SBP 6.5 (3.3, 9.7), DBP -3.4 (-5.2, -1.6), HR 3.4 (0.1, 3.5), 8-OHdG 8.1 (0.7, 8.8). The increment is each mode's own IQR, computed as stated formula [β × IQR × M] × 100% (M endpoint mean); no per-10 µg/m3 or absolute values; pooled IQR not stated.

4. Significant (asterisked, CI excludes zero): scooter SBP, HR, 8-OHdG; walking SBP, HR, 8-OHdG; bus SBP, 8-OHdG; car 8-OHdG; respirator-walking 8-OHdG; pooled 8-OHdG. Not significant: subway all four; car SBP, DBP, HR; scooter DBP; respirator SBP, DBP, HR; pooled SBP, DBP, HR; bus DBP. Unstarred but CI below zero: walking DBP (-3.4; -5.2, -1.6) and bus HR (-2.3; -3.3, -1.3), not discussed by the authors.

5. Adjusted for age, sex, BMI, order of measurement, 1-h temperature, humidity and noise (plus mode in Model 1). Noise measured and controlled. Physical exertion not measured (authors cite it as confounding). NO2, VOCs and ozone unavailable; CO not mentioned (the Introduction cites a CO study only). ETS and time-activity recorded by questionnaire but not used as covariates.

6. Authors attribute low subway/car PM2.5 to ventilation and in-vehicle filtration ('the ventilation status of the vehicle is an important factor for TRAP exposure'). The source is only 'traffic-related'; no tailpipe measurement or source apportionment. Scooters/motorcycles are named in the abstract recommendation, Section 5 and when citing other studies (Li et al. 2017).
7. Not assessed. BP/HR were recorded every 15 min during the commute hour and urine collected after each measurement; the delay, any follow-up, persistence or reversibility are not reported.

8. Limitations (p.4): 'The major limitation of our panel study was the biological explanation of the short-term effects of PM2.5 on cardiovascular endpoints.'; 'whether short-term and small fluctuations of cardiovascular endpoints are associated with higher risks of cardiovascular diseases clinically remains unknown.'; 'The physical activities were completely different among commuters of different commuting modes, resulting in confounding effects.'; unmeasured NO2, VOCs and ozone 'might bias our study results toward the null'; findings 'may not be completely extrapolated to other locations'. Conclusions: abstract 'We concluded that traffic-related PM2.5 was associated with cardiovascular effects. We encourage commuters to commute using public rapid transit systems instead of riding scooters/motorcycles during rush hours.' Section 5: 'The usage of facemasks should be considered for walking commuters during rush hours.'
